catalog_quote: [p.161, §3.31 Phonological Rules (Language A)] Primary stress is assigned to the penultimate vowel of underlying phonological words. [fn.3] A phonological word is enclosed by # or [+word] boundary. [p.162] Primary stress rule A.P.1 [+syl] → [1 stress] / __ ((C) V) [-segment, -morpheme] i.e., primary stress is assigned on the penultimate vowel of a word and to the last vowel if the word is monosyllabic. The rule A.P.1 as specified would not assign stress with just a morpheme boundary, but would assign it with word and pause boundary. Secondary stress rule A.P.2 ... i.e., secondary stress is placed on the second vowel preceding the primary stressed vowel. Both rules A.P.1 and A.P.2 must be understood as assigning primary and secondary stress within word boundary; therefore the rule works also across morpheme boundary as seen in the examples given in (7). [p.203, §3.51 Phonological Rules (Language C)] Yanomamɨ has fewer phonological rules than Yanomam but it has no rules which Yanomam does not have. Rules which do not apply for Yanomamɨ are omitted but the rule numbers follow the sequence established for Yanam and Yanomam. Stress placement C.P.1 Same as B.P.1 and A.P.1 C.P.2 Same as B.P.2 and A.P.2 [p.208, §3.61] While in the other languages stress was predictable only in terms of phonological boundaries, in Sanɨma syntactic categories (nouns and verbs) as well as boundaries seem to be necessary.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Yanomamɨ is predictable and non-contrastive: primary stress falls on the penultimate vowel of the phonological word (a word bounded by # / pause; vowel sequences count per vowel, e.g. maáma 'stone'), on the only vowel of monosyllables; the rule ignores morpheme boundaries, so suffixed words are stressed on their penultimate vowel (šáma 'tapir' but šamá-nə 'tapir-readers').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Rule A.P.2 (= C.P.2): secondary stress on the second vowel preceding the primary-stressed vowel (one unstressed syllable in between), e.g. Yanam kàri-hámə, nakàma-thókə.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated specifically for Language C. For Yanomam (B) an additional rule B.P.1a shifts primary stress to the final vowel of [+V] words (verbs, adjectivals, adverbials) under focus or emphatic speech (p.190); §3.51 lists only rules that apply to C and does not list B.P.1a. Sanɨma (D) differs (category-sensitive, cliticised pronouns). In the sister language Yanomama of Papiu (yano1262), Ferreira 2017 §2.5 reports the same penultimate default with final stress when the singulative =a / classifier =u is the last enclitic.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word enclosed by # or pause boundary (fn.3 p.161); words uttered in isolation 'have pause boundaries and function as sentences'; nouns can stand alone as phonological words but verbs must carry pronouns and suffixes, and stress is computed over the whole suffixed word. Stress is counted in vowels (penultimate vowel), not syllables with long nuclei.
new_statements.identity_note: Migliazza 1972 treats four Yanomama languages; his 'Language C = Yanomamɨ' (west-southwest: Padamo, Ocamo, Manaviche, upper Orinoco, Parima east of the Butaa, possibly south to the Marauiá/Cauaburí headwaters; ~6,000 speakers; the variety of Barker's and Lizot's materials, i.e. Chagnon's 'Yanomamö') is Glottolog yano1261. His stress rules for C (p.203) are stated by cross-reference to the Yanam (A, = nina1238) and Yanomam (B, = yano1262) rules on pp.161-162, 190, and p.208 confirms that in A, B and C 'stress was predictable only in terms of phonological boundaries'. Two identity cautions: (i) Migliazza & Grimes 1961 'Shiriana phonology', which Glottolog files under yano1261, actually describes Shiriana of the upper Uraricaá = Ninam (nina1238); (ii) Ferreira 2017 (also downloaded) describes Yanomama of Papiu = yano1262 Yanomám, a sister language, and is corroborating context only.

new_statements.quote: L'accent tonique primaire [+accent] tombe sur l'avant-dernière syllabe du mot phonologique, l'accent tonique secondaire [+accent₁], de deux en deux syllabes, à partir de l'accent primaire [...] L'accent tonique secondaire est légèrement moins haut que l'accent tonique primaire. Cette accentuation n'a pas de fonction contrastive. Par contre, sa fonction démarcative permet de définir une unité, le mot phonologique (#) [...] [p. 80:] On ne confondra pas cet accent tonique et l'accent d'intensité, qui tombe généralement sur la première syllabe du mot phonologique. Ces deux accents ne sont donc pas toujours portés par la même syllabe.
new_statements.translation: The primary tonic accent [+accent] falls on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word, the secondary tonic accent [+accent1] every second syllable counting from the primary accent [...] The secondary tonic accent is slightly lower (in pitch) than the primary tonic accent. This accentuation has no contrastive function. On the other hand, its demarcative function makes it possible to define a unit, the phonological word (#) [...] [p. 80:] This tonic accent must not be confused with the intensity accent, which generally falls on the first syllable of the phonological word. The two accents are therefore not always borne by the same syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog rule (penultimate stress) and as Migliazza 1972 (penultimate vowel of the phonological word): agrees on penult. Refines by (a) formalising a secondary accent on every other syllable leftward from the penult, (b) stating that accent is non-contrastive and purely demarcative of the phonological word, (c) noting that the penultimate 'accent tonique' is a pitch prominence while a distinct 'accent d'intensité' (loudness) generally sits on the first syllable, (d) listing the imperative/emphatic and intonational exceptions above. Point (c) is a nuance the catalog's single 'stress' label does not capture but does not change the penultimate placement of the primary toni…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary tonic accent (realised as high pitch, 'ton haut') on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word; rule (ACC): [+syl] -> [+accent] / __[(C)V]#. Secondary accents (slightly lower pitch) on every second syllable leftward from the primary, rule (ACC1). Accent is non-contrastive and serves only to demarcate the phonological word, which includes incorporated nominals and suffixes (waro # ya / naka-ma vs ya / waro / naka-ma, p. 80). A separate intensity (loudness) accent generally falls on the first syllable, so in odd-syllable words pitch peak and loudness peak are on different syllables ('hikári, 'kayúri, p. 80) and coincide in even-syllable words (masi'hótō).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: secondary tonic accent every other syllable leftward from the penult (ACC1), slightly lower in pitch than the primary; examples wáyāpáxī 'squirrel sp.', hōáxī 'capuchin monkey', xámā 'tapir', pátā 'big' (p. 79); derivation kó-rayó-ū p. 87.
new_statements.exceptions: Remark 1 (p. 80): in injunctions (imperatives) the tonic and intensity accents always coincide on the penultimate syllable, uttered with fairly strong intensity and relatively high pitch (hi'pë-kɨ! 'give it!'); same for emphasis and prohibition, with lengthening of the accented vowel. Remark 2: polar questions have a slightly more rising intonation on the penult than the affirmative; wh-questions lack this. Remark 3 (p. 81): in a subordinate clause preceding the main clause the intonation rises clearly on the LAST syllable of the verbal word (sequential ha+..-nɨ). Remark 4: a short pause is possible between phonological words, never inside one. Also p. 62 (§3.10): syllable pattern (C)V regardless of whether the syllable is unstressed or stressed ('atone ou tonique').
new_statements.identity_note: Ramirez 1994 describes the speech of the Xamatauteri, a community of about 200 people on the Marauiá river, Amazonas, Brazil (§1.6, p. 20), which he classifies as dialect 'Yoc-sud'; his Yoc (Yoc-sud / Yoc-nord / Yoc-f) corresponds to Migliazza's Language C = Yanomamɨ, as opposed to Yor (Yanomam, yano1262). So the work is about yano1261, Brazilian (Marauiá) variety.

tone_statements.quote: L'accent tonique primaire (+accent) tombe sur l'avant-dernière syllabe du mot phonologique, l'accent tonique secondaire (+accent 1], de deux en deux syllabes, à partir de l'accent primaire # xâmâ # tapir # wâyâpâxï # [...] avec : â ton haut à ton moyen L'accent tonique secondaire est légèrement moins haut que l'accent tonique primaire. Cette accentuation n'a pas de fonction contrastive. Par contre, sa fonction démarcative permet de définir une unité, le mot phonologique (#) [...] On ne confondra pas cet accent tonique et l'accent d'intensité, qui tombe généralement sur la première syllabe du mot phonologique.
tone_statements.translation: The primary tonic (pitch) accent [+accent] falls on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word, the secondary tonic accent [+accent1] on every second syllable counting from the primary accent: # xâmâ # 'tapir', # wâyâpâxï # [...] with: â high tone, à mid tone. The secondary tonic accent is slightly less high than the primary tonic accent. This accentuation has no contrastive function. On the other hand, its demarcative function makes it possible to define a unit, the phonological word (#) [...] This tonic accent must not be confused with the intensity accent, which generally falls on the first syllable of the phonological word.

Word order and intonation 'n'ont que des fonctions discursiv…

sources.citation: Migliazza, Ernest & Joseph E. Grimes. 1961. Shiriana phonology. Anthropological Linguistics 3(6): 31-41.
sources.note: Describes Shiriana of the upper Uraricaá (= Ninam, nina1238, not yano1261 despite Glottolog's filing): non-phonemic stress; every foot has one loud stress, on the penult of a pause-group-final foot and on the ultima of other feet; a reduced stress on the second syllable preceding the loud stress (pp.33-35).

sources.citation: Ferreira, Helder Perri. 2017. Yanomama Clause Structure. PhD dissertation, Radboud University Nijmegen (LOT 475), vol. 1.
sources.note: SISTER LANGUAGE (Yanomama of Papiu = yano1262): §2.5 pp.52ff 'Stress is not a distinctive feature of the YMA lexical phonology.. the stress tends to fall on the penultimate syllable at the lexical level', in roots and derived/inflected stems; exceptions: singulative =a, classifier =u and one other enclitic take final stress when they are the last enclitic; clause-final particles attract prosodic stress.
